subject: orthopaedics
title: Injuries around the elbow in children and adults

steps.tx: Elbow injuries are common in children. **Supracondylar fracture** of the humerus is the most frequent, peaking between 5 and 8 years. Most result from a fall on the outstretched hand, which forces the elbow into hyperextension. Extension type accounts for about 95 to 98 percent of cases, so it is the pattern to know for exams.

Most result from a fall on the outstretched hand, which forces the elbow into hyperextension. Extension type accounts for about ninety five to ninety eight percent of cases, so it is the pattern to know for exams.

steps.tx: The **Gartland classification** grades extension-type fractures. Type I is non-displaced. Type II is displaced with an intact posterior cortex, and is split into rotationally stable (IIA) and unstable (IIB). Type III is completely displaced with no cortical contact. Closed reduction is attempted for types I and II, but not for type III, which usually needs closed reduction and percutaneous pinning.
steps.say: The Gartland classification grades extension type fractures. Type one is non displaced. Type two is displaced with an intact posterior cortex, and is split into rotationally stable and unstable subtypes. Type three is completely displaced with no cortical contact. Closed reduction is attempted for types one and two, but not for type three, which usually needs closed reduction and percutaneous pinning.

steps.tx: Adequacy of reduction is checked with the **Baumann angle**, compared with the uninjured side. A difference of more than 5 degrees is unacceptable. The anterior humeral line should also pass through the capitellum. Neurovascular status must be checked before and after reduction. The **brachial artery** is the vessel most often injured, because the sharp proximal spike can traumatise it. Urgent reduction and reassessment are needed if perfusion is poor.

steps.tx: Nerve injury occurs in about 5 to 19 percent of supracondylar fractures, more often in type III. The **median nerve** is most often involved, followed by the radial nerve. Most are neuropraxic and recover within weeks to months. Vascular compromise can lead to **Volkmann ischaemic contracture**, so any increasing pain or tense compartment needs urgent fasciotomy consideration.
steps.say: Nerve injury occurs in about five to nineteen percent of supracondylar fractures, more often in type three. The median nerve is most often involved, followed by the radial nerve. Most are neuropraxic and recover within weeks to months. Vascular compromise can lead to Volkmann ischaemic contracture, so any increasing pain or tense compartment needs urgent fasciotomy consideration.

steps.tx: Malunion is the commonest complication of supracondylar fracture and causes **cubitus varus**, the gunstock deformity. The distal fragment tilts medially and rotates internally. It is mainly a cosmetic problem. Treatment is a corrective supracondylar osteotomy, usually the lateral closing wedge (French) type, deferred until skeletal maturity. In contrast, **cubitus valgus** follows lateral condyle fractures and can lead to **tardy ulnar nerve palsy**, managed by ulnar nerve decompression or anterior transposition.

steps.tx: Other elbow injuries to recognise are the **pulled elbow**, the **posterior elbow dislocation** and the **Monteggia** pattern. A pulled elbow in a young child is treated by manual reduction, usually with supination and flexion. In posterior dislocation, the olecranon is the most prominent point and the three bony points are reversed. Closed reduction is followed by an above-elbow slab at 90 degrees of flexion for about 3 weeks.
